stops.name: Domrémy, the church of Saint-Rémy
stops.campa: The little church of Saint-Rémy stands hard against the garden wall of Jacques d'Arc's house, so near that a girl at her spinning can hear the bell and cross to Mass in a few steps. Here Jehanne is christened; here she kneels so often that the sexton must chide her for coming to church too much; here she loves the sound of the bells and gives the bellringer wool and cakes to ring them well. This is the ground her right ear turns to when, in a few years, the first voice will come out of the summer noon, from the right side, toward the church.
stops.quote: I loved and still love God, Our Lady, and all the saints in heaven... I went willingly and often to church, and confessed my sins.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, sessions of 22 and 24 February 1431

stops.name: Domrémy, the Tree of Bourlemont, the Fair May
stops.campa: On Laetare Sunday the young folk of Domrémy walk out to the great beech on the lands of the lords of Bourlemont, near the Bois Chenu: the Ladies' Tree, the Fairies' Tree, where the ladies of faery danced in the old time. Here, two hundred years gone, old Joffrey de Bourlémont, home from Jerusalem, told the dancing children of the Holy Land and the dragons. Jehanne goes with the other girls; they bring bread, sing and dance, cut the fair May and hang garlands for the image of Our Lady of Domrémy. Her godmother says she has seen the fairies here. Jehanne, as far as she knows, never has.
stops.quote: Fairly near Domrémy there is a tree called the Ladies' Tree, and others call it the Fairies' Tree... It is a big tree, a beech, from which they get the fair May, in French le beau may; and it belongs, it is said, to Pierre de Bourlemont, knight. I sometimes went there with the other girls, and made garlands for Our Lady of Domrémy... I never saw the fairies at the tree, that I know of.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 24 February 1431

stops.name: Domrémy, la Fontaine des Fiévreux
stops.campa: Beside the Ladies' Tree runs the spring the village calls the Fontaine des Fiévreux, the fountain of the fever-sick, whose water is said to heal them. It was Joffrey de Bourlémont, home from Jerusalem, who built the well for the spring. On the Fountains Sunday the children come down from the dancing to drink, and the sick who can still walk draw its water and are made whole. Jehanne drinks with the others and has seen the fevered come; whether cured she cannot say, only that they came and believed. Between beech and healing water lies the whole enchantment of her childhood, the last of it before the light.
stops.quote: Near the tree there is a fountain; and people sick of the fever drink of this fountain and seek its water to restore their health. I have seen them come; but whether they were cured or not, I do not know.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 24 February 1431

stops.name: Domrémy, the Bois Chenu and the prophecy
stops.campa: Above the tree and the fountain rises the hoary oak wood the country calls the Bois Chenu: nemus canutum, the wood of the grey oaks. An old prophecy runs through the marches of Lorraine, laid to Merlin and to Bede and to Marie d'Avignon: that France, ruined by a woman, shall be saved by a virgin come out of the Bois Chenu for the healing of the nations. Jehanne herds her father's beasts on this hillside and hears the saying, as all the village hears it, and does not yet know that it is spoken of her. On this slope the basilica of the visions will one day stand.

stops.name: Domrémy, her father's garden
stops.campa: A summer noon in her father's garden, hard by the church of Saint-Rémy. Jehanne, a girl of the village who spins and sews and yields to no woman of Rouen in needlework, hears a voice from God on her right side, toward the church, and with the voice comes a great light. It is Saint Michael, and he does not come alone: Saints Catherine and Margaret will follow, crowned in rich and precious crowns. She is very much afraid. The voice tells her to be good, to go to church, and, in time, that she must go into France. She tells no one.
stops.quote: I was thirteen when I had a voice from God to help me govern myself. And the first time I was very much afraid. This voice came about noon, in summer, in my father's garden... I heard it on the right side, toward the church; and rarely do I hear it without a light.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 22 February 1431

stops.name: Domrémy, the Ladies' Tree and the Bois Chenu
stops.campa: On Laetare Sunday the young people of Domrémy go out to the great beech called the Ladies' Tree, near the healing spring. Jehanne goes with them, hangs garlands on the boughs for the image of Our Lady, sings, and eats with the others. The fairies frequented the tree in the old time; her godmother has seen them, and has told her the tree's romance: the Seigneur Pierre de Bourlément and a lady called Fée, met beneath these boughs. But Jehanne, since she has known that she must go into France, takes little part in the games. The prophecy of Merlin says a maid shall come from the Bois Chenu.
stops.quote: Quite near Domrémy there is a tree called the Ladies' Tree... I sometimes made garlands there with the other girls for the image of Our Lady of Domrémy... I never saw a fairy at the tree, so far as I know.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 24 February 1431

stops.name: Vaucouleurs, first audience with Robert de Baudricourt
stops.campa: About Ascension-tide, Jehanne persuades her uncle Durand Laxart to bring her to Vaucouleurs, the last tower of the king's obedience on the Meuse. In the castle hall she stands before the captain Robert de Baudricourt in her patched red dress and tells him the kingdom belongs not to the Dauphin but to her Lord, who wills the Dauphin to be made king and to hold it in trust; she herself will lead him to his anointing. Baudricourt laughs and tells Laxart to take her home to her father and box her ears. She goes home. The voice does not release her.
stops.quote: Was it not said of old that France would be ruined by a woman, and afterward restored by a virgin from the marches of Lorraine?
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Durand Laxart and Catherine Le Royer, rehabilitation trial (1456)

stops.name: Neufchâteau, the flight before the Burgundians
stops.campa: In July the riders of Antoine de Vergy sweep up the valley of the Meuse and burn against Vaucouleurs; the village church of Domrémy is set alight. The whole village drives its beasts south to the walled town of Neufchâteau, and Jehanne with her father and mother lodges about a fortnight at the inn of a good woman called La Rousse, helping in the house and keeping the animals. Here too a young man cites her before the court at Toul, claiming a promise of marriage; she never made one, and swears it, and the case is dismissed. She returns to a scorched village.
stops.quote: For fear of the Burgundians I left home and went to Neufchâteau, to the house of a woman called La Rousse, where I stayed about a fortnight.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 22 February 1431

stops.name: Vaucouleurs, the return, at the house of the Le Royers
stops.campa: In the dead of winter Jehanne comes again to Vaucouleurs, lodging three weeks with the wheelwright Henri Le Royer and his wife Catherine, spinning by the fire and climbing daily to hear mass in the crypt chapel of Notre-Dame-des-Voûtes. The town begins to believe. The squire Jean de Metz finds her in her poor red dress and asks what she is doing here; her answer converts him on the spot, and he pledges his hand that he will lead her to the king. The people of Vaucouleurs buy her a horse and men's clothes: tunic, hose, boots, the dress of the road.
stops.quote: I must be at the King's side, though I wear my legs down to the knees. For no one in the world — kings, dukes, nor the King of Scotland's daughter — can recover the kingdom of France; nor is there succour to be had but from me, although I would rather spin beside my poor mother, for this is not my station. But I must go, and I must do it, because my Lord wills it.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Jean de Metz, rehabilitation trial (1456)

stops.name: Nancy, before Charles II, Duke of Lorraine
stops.campa: The old Duke of Lorraine, sick and curious, sends a safe-conduct for the maid whose fame has crossed his marches. Jehanne rides to Nancy under his seal, pausing to pray at the great shrine of Saint Nicholas at Saint-Nicolas-de-Port, patron of Lorraine. The duke asks about his health, hoping for a healer. She tells him plainly she knows nothing of that, counsels him to amend his life and be reconciled with his wife, and asks instead for his son-in-law René and men to take her into France, promising to pray for him. He gives her four francs and a black horse.
stops.quote: The duke questioned me about his health; but of that I told him I knew nothing... I told him to give me his son and men to take me into France, and that I would pray God for his health.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 22 February 1431

stops.name: Vaucouleurs, the Porte de France, the departure
stops.campa: On the twelfth of February, the very day the French fall at Rouvray, Jehanne tells Baudricourt that the Dauphin's arms have this day suffered great loss near Orléans; when the courier confirms it days later, the captain resists no more. Now, toward evening, she rides out through the Porte de France with six companions: Jean de Metz, Bertrand de Poulengy, their servants, the archer Richard, the king's courier Colet de Vienne. Her hair is cut round, in black and grey. Baudricourt has girt a sword on her and speaks the words of the tradition: 'Go, go, and come what may.' Eleven nights of enemy country lie ahead.
stops.quote: I do not fear the soldiers, for my road is made open to me; and if the soldiers come, I have God, my Lord, who will know how to clear the route that leads to messire the Dauphin. It was for this that I was born.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Jean de Metz and Bertrand de Poulengy, rehabilitation trial (1456)

stops.name: Abbey of Saint-Urbain, the first night
stops.campa: The little troop rides by night and hides by day, fording rivers swollen with the February thaw, avoiding the bridges where Burgundian and English garrisons watch. The first shelter is the abbey of Saint-Urbain on the Marne, whose abbot is kinsman to Baudricourt. The men sleep armed, lying beside her, and afterward swear they felt no stir of desire toward her, only awe, as toward something holy. She grieves that they cannot hear mass on the road; her companions dare not stop in hostile towns. She tells them not to fear: she has her counsel, and God clears the way.
